lignes.texte: The world is staring down the barrel of a digital blackout.
For over a century, astrophysicists thought solar storms could only brew deep in the
sun’s core. Because of that, the multi-billion dollar data centers powering the AI revolution
were built unprotected. They were built on a lie.
Scientists have caught invisible plasma whirlpools tearing the sun’s outer crust.
And they strike faster and harder than we thought. A single hit won’t cause a flicker of your lights.
It will collapse our global infrastructure. And it’s already too late to stop it.
As AI begins to take over everyday life, the global data centers that power them are
on track to double between 2026 and 2030. Just one of these facilities can easily draw upwards
of 100 megawatts of continuous power, enough to drain an entire mid-sized town. Worse, millions
of critical systems, from global logistics and financial systems are hooked into them.
But the demands of the AI network have been plugged into a grid that is fundamentally flawed.
In recent decades, we have reshaped the rules of electrical engineering. To combat
the climate crisis, high-voltage networks are increasingly shifting away from fossil
fuels and hydroelectric facilities. Instead, they’re moving toward inverter-based renewable
energy, like wind and solar power. It’s a huge victory for the planet,
but a massive mistake for our security. Because by abandoning the old school
power plants, the main shield of the grid has been stripped away… the mechanical inertia.
The old system made use of heavy, rapidly spinning mechanical turbines essentially
acting like giant shock absorbers. They soaked up and smoothed out the random voltage surges
or sudden spikes in frequency that can occur randomly, including solar weather phenomena.
But green energy grids don’t spin. They don’t have the ability to
absorb a massive electrical shock. In essence, in trying to save our planet,
we’ve torn down our own defenses at the exact moment our digital economy
became reliant on an uninterrupted flow of power. And that flow could be interrupted at any second.
When the sun unleashes an explosive eruption, it launches two major attacks on our planet.
The first is a solar flare. An intense burst of electromagnetic radiation travels at the speed of
light, slamming into the Earth in just 8 minutes. The flare ionizes Earth’s upper atmosphere,
knocking aviation, maritime, and emergency communications offline.
Satellites and GPS signals are blinded as the atmosphere is flooded with X-rays and
extreme levels of ultraviolet radiation. But the second attack is the killer.
The coronal mass ejection, or CME. This is a massive wave of magnetized plasma
and embedded magnetic fields blasted straight from the Sun's outer atmosphere. Packed with billions
of tons of solar material, CMEs travel up to 1,900 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per
second). This means it can take several days to reach the Earth’s atmosphere.
That’s the good news. The bad news is they are
infinitely more destructive. When a CME collides with our
protective magnetic field, they can violently compress it, triggering geomagnetic storms.
This forces the electrical currents straight out of the ground below our feet. Those rogue
currents flood into high-voltage substations and surge along long-distance power lines, causing
widespread blackouts and transformer damage. At the exact same time, high energy particles
hit our satellite networks, degrading orbital tracking and killing off GPS.
Humanity got a glimpse of this power back in September 1859,
during the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history: the Carrington Event.
This was before the internet, AI, and green-energy power grids. But people still saw the effects.
Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed. Operators suffered electric
shocks. Telegraph pylons spontaneously threw sparks out causing several fires to break out.
Experts believe that if a severe Carrington-class solar storm were to strike Earth today,
the effects would be unprecedented. Some models suggest the direct damages could reach
up to $2 trillion, roughly 15 times the initial destruction caused by Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
And unlike a bad storm, tornado, or tsunami, a Carrington-style
space event would act on a planetary scale. Energy networks across large parts of the
world would be disabled in a matter of seconds. Paralyzed power lines would only be the beginning.
The extra high voltage (EHV) transformers, which control the flow of power between plants,
substations, and national grids would be especially vulnerable. Weighing
several hundred tons each, these monstrous components form the backbone of 21st century
electrical grids… and they’re not easy to make. Rather than being mass produced on assembly lines,
EHV transformers are custom-engineered and highly-specialized. Even in a booming economy,
it can take several years to build a single unit. If a solar storm fries hundreds of these giant
transformers simultaneously across the globe, the supply chain quickly collapses.
Because of this, the effects of a Carrington-scale CME wouldn’t
just last for a few months, it could take a decade to rebuild our energy infrastructure.
Vast swathes of the population - as well as large parts of the
tech economy - would be forced to operate without a stable source of electrical power.
So, how did it get to this? How could the world’s top engineers allow our entire
civilization to be built on a knife edge? They had no idea the danger was real.
For over a century, the global power grid was designed around a massive scientific blindspot.
Astrophysicists believed that the solar dynamo - the “engine” of the sun’s magnetic field - only
operated deep inside the solar core, tens of thousands of miles beneath the surface.
Under this“deep core” model, space weather moved slowly and predictably. Scientists thought they
could always stay one step ahead, tracking solar storms days and weeks in advance to protect Earth.
Unfortunately, the model was wrong. Or, to be more exact, it was incomplete.
While everyone was busy focusing on the sun’s core, they completely missed the
chaotic high-speed physics unraveling across its surface. And this was partly because
they were working blind. Back in the late 1860s,
two of the top physicists of the time, Lord Kelvin and Hermann von Helmholtz,
came up with a concept called Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI). It happens when 2
layers of fluid or gas scrape past each other at different speeds or in different directions,
creating violent rolling disturbances at the edge. It’s like when wind whips across the surface of a
calm lake, causing ripples forming and waves breaking. We can observe this phenomenon in
atmospheric cloud formations and even the planetary atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn.
About a century later, solar physicists realized this same violent churning should
apply to the superheated plasma ocean that covers the surface of the sun.
The problem was that they didn’t have a powerful enough telescope to prove it.
Without empirical evidence to rely on, the scientific community still treated the “deep
core” model as absolute law. They assumed that any surface plasma dynamics were the side-effects
of more powerful magnetic flows far below them. And the wider world bought into that assumption.
Decisions about energy infrastructure were made by people who thought solar storms were
easy to predict, track and survive. It’s only now, in 2026, that this
long-standing myth is beginning to crumble. It began when researchers at the Massachusetts
Institute of Technology, or MIT, developed highly precise numerical models of solar plasma flow.
The team realized that small plasma disturbances in the sun’s upper layers were generating powerful
magnetic field patterns. In other words, it wasn’t the core causing solar storms
and flares, but the surface. The team had a theory,
but they still needed proof. And the only way to get it was to capture
detailed pictures of the sun’s surface, which was something that had been almost impossible.
The sun is approximately 93 million miles (149.6 million km) away from us.
Its visible surface - known as the photosphere - is a violent, bubbling landscape, covered in
granules. A single granule can measure over 1,200 miles (1,931 km) across, and is made up
of superheated plasma. This rises up from below, cools at the surface, and sinks back down at the
granule’s boundaries. If the wave-like structures caused by KHI existed along those edges, they’d
measure around 40 miles (64 km) from peak to peak. Trying to spot something of that size from nearly
100 million miles (161 million km) away is like asking someone to identify a single coin from a
distance of 100 miles (161 km) Conventional ground-based
telescopes didn’t stand a chance. So, scientists built a better one.
Sitting 10,000 feet (3,000 meters) above sea level in Hawaii and costing nearly $350 million,
it’s called the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope. Equipped with a 13 foot (3.96 meter) mirror,
it’s capable of collecting around 7 times more light than any previous model. And in 2021,
it came online, instantly providing some of the clearest images of the sun ever seen.
In 2026, researchers pointed it towards a particularly active region of the
sun’s photosphere in order to test a high speed “Fast Cam.”
In just a few minutes, it proved its worth and shattered a century-long myth,
capturing clear images of 47 curling wave crests along the edges of plasma granules:
clear evidence of Kelvin Helmholtz Instability on the solar surface.
But this isn’t like wind blowing across a lake on Earth.
The sun’s superheated plasma is interwoven with huge magnetic fields that act like rubber bands.
They exert a continuous force that fights against the waves, trying to keep the plasma in place.
For a wave to form and curl across the sun’s surface, fast-moving plasma has to move across
a slower-moving stream with such force that it overwhelms the magnetic fields. The result is
terrifying. Instead of ripples, magnetized plasma waves stretch upward into curling whirlpool-like
vortices, rising hundreds of feet into the air. Millions of these whirlpools are constantly
forming, spinning, and collapsing. And that wasn’t the only discovery.
In October 2025, the telescope captured the first physical evidence of another threat: small-scale
torsional Alfven waves twisting across the sun’s upper atmosphere. First theorized in the 1940s
by the Swedish engineer and physicist, Hannes Alfven, these waves are magnetic fluctuations that
act like high voltage conduits, throwing massive amounts of energy along the sun’s magnetic fields.
Before this breakthrough, scientists could only see large swaying movements across arch-like
plasma structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, known as coronal loops. But it was only with the
Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope that they were able to isolate them and see them for
what they really were: high-speed magnetic corkscrews, twisting and turning plasma
back and forth at ultra-fast speeds. The discoveries of Alfven waves and
KHI phenomena on the solar surface helped solve a mystery that had plagued scientists
for decades: the Coronal Heating Paradox. The outer atmosphere of the sun - the corona - can
reach up to 3.6 million degrees Fahrenheit (2 million degrees Celsius), yet the photosphere
stays at a far cooler 9,900 degrees Fahrenheit (5,500 degrees Celsius). It makes no sense and
has stumped scientists for years. The newly-discovered waves and
whirlpools change everything. As millions of plasma whirlpools
rage along granule boundaries, their movements drag magnetic fields together, a process known
as “flux braiding”. It’s like twisting strands of magnetic rope into tightly contorted knots. Then,
as the magnetic tension builds up inside those knots, the tangled lines snap and reconnect,
releasing enormous and continuous bursts of energy that heat up the outer atmosphere.
Unfortunately, these discoveries also revealed a frightening new threat for life on Earth.
They rewrote the rules of how solar systems are triggered.
Before then, classical space weather models suggested that solar flares and CMEs needed
a gradual, slow, and predictable build-up. But the discovery of KHI proves that violent waves
screaming across the solar surface are the real agitators. This means
that solar storms are nowhere near as predictable as previously believed.
The implications of this are enormous. And the timing couldn’t be worse.
At the very moment that human civilization has basically plugged itself into an unshielded
electrical grid, we’re realizing it could be wiped out without warning. There’s nothing
we can do to stop it. And the window we have to minimize the losses is closing.
We thought we’d have ample warning time, allowing us to adjust network voltages and isolate the
most vulnerable substations. But that’s not how it works.
A CME could come at almost any time. It would release huge clouds of radiated
energy without sounding the alarms beforehand. When that wave collides with our atmosphere,
it will kick start a catastrophic change. Currents would surge up and slam into a modern grid
unable to cope with them. The iron cores of EHV transformers would become overloaded and internal
operating temperatures would rise in a matter of seconds. Insulating oil would bubble and boil,
structural components would degrade, and entire power stations go up into flames.
We would be starting down the barrel of a digital blackout.
There’s no telling how the wider world would cope with that. Industries would struggle to function
without power. Countries would decide which among them get first call on the first custom-engineered
EHV transformers to be completed. What makes this entire idea much
more concerning is that we may be entering an era in which severe solar storms are about to
become much more frequent and dangerous. The sun operates on an 11-year cycle,
but historical records and recent satellite data also suggest that there are additional
patterns at play. One of those patterns is known as the Centennial Gleissberg Cycle - a spinning
wheel of solar storm intensity that rises and falls every 80 to 100 years. Analysis reveals
that the sun has just finished the “fall” of that cycle and is about to start rising back up again.
In other words, for the last few decades, while humanity was building the internet, satellites,
continental power grids, and investigating artificial intelligence, our sun was going
through a kind of “quiet phase” or “cosmic lull.” Now, it’s roaring back to life, which may explain
why we’ve already started to see some serious space weather over the last couple of years.
The “Gannon Storm” of 2024 involved a highly active sunspot - 17 times the
diameter of Earth - emitting no fewer than 8 CMEs, several of which were directed towards Earth,
triggering G5-level - the highest level - geomagnetic storm conditions and one of
the largest satellite migrations in history. Based on this evidence, some experts believe
that the decades ahead of us will see a clear spike in solar activity. This will
increase the odds of severe geomagnetic storms occurring across our world.
Humanity is edging closer to the edge of a cliff. Our technology is moving faster than ever,
but the infrastructure that powers has never been so fragile. We are completely
exposed just as our local star is entering a new era of heightened violent activity,.
And we’ve just uncovered the truth. But perhaps, with that new data at their disposal,
scientists can begin to understand the chaotic physics of the sun’s surface waves. If they move
quick enough, they might be able to build stronger, more accurate forecasting models.
Models that allow them to pinpoint the moments when flares and CMEs are most likely to occur.
Until then, humanity will have to live in hope that the next “Carrington Event” is
still several years away. It might be.
But one thing’s for sure: as our star begins its next active chapter,
the time we have left to insulate our infrastructure is rapidly running out.
There’s still so much we don’t know about our own star, including its
surroundings. And those blind spots might be deadly. Watch “What's Directly Above
And Below The Sun?” to find out what’s lurking in the void. Or click on this.
